song.title: It’s A Spring Thing!
song.author: Mark and Helen Johnson
song.summary: Definitely a song to make you smile! With a cumulative chorus, highly descriptive verses and a really fun harmony echo, there’s plenty here to enjoy. Clarity of diction will only enhance the satisfaction of singing the rhymes and alliteration.
song.teachingTips:
• There are lots of words in this song that all need to be sung clearly, so start with a warm-up that focuses on diction such as Peter Piper from S!ng Warm-Ups.
  • Try to keep the tempo steady and avoid rushing, especially through the faster words.
  • Notice that the quavers in the melody are performed ‘swung’, i.e. with the first quaver lengthened and the second quaver shortened. This gives the song its distinctive jazzy feel.

assembly.title: Super Seeds
assembly.description: This assembly encourages us to look at the potential of seeds for new life and growth and also provides an opportunity to explore our own potential.

assembly.title: Light and Colour
assembly.description: This assembly encourages us to open our eyes to the colours of springtime, talking about our favourite colours, noticing the extra daylight and appreciating nature's use of colour and light.

assembly.title: Extra Energy
assembly.description: What wakes you up in the morning? From birdsong to sprouting leaves and Easter eggs, this assembly helps us to celebrate all the energy of springtime.

assembly.title: Turning Over a New Leaf
assembly.description: This assembly looks at new leaves and growth in nature and helps us all to look within ourselves to see where we might want to ‘turn over a new leaf’ too.

assembly.title: Metamorphosis
assembly.description: Looking at change and understanding that there are things to be enjoyed at every stage of life.

assembly.title: People Who Care
assembly.description: The ideal assembly to help us to focus on, appreciate and celebrate all those who help and care for us.

assembly.title: The World Around
assembly.description: From the tallest trees, to the something you can only see with a microscope, this assembly encourages us to notice, appreciate and be thankful for the world around us.

assembly.title: It’s Challenging
assembly.description: By looking at changes in nature, this assembly helps us to explore change and how it can sometimes be difficult.

assembly.title: Happy Endings
assembly.description: This assembly explores setbacks we might encounter in our lives and the characteristics needed to overcome them.

assembly.title: Feeling Hopeful
assembly.description: This assembly explores the meaning of hope and what it will take to realize our ambitions for the future.

assembly.title: Feeling Awake
assembly.description: This assembly uses The Parable of the Sower to reflect on what is needed to be ‘awake and ready for action’ in school.

assembly.title: Feeling Good
assembly.description: This assembly explores the uniqueness of human beings and how we can help others to feel more valuable.

resources.title: Spring Spoken Chorus
resources.content:
[{"key":"a0d7ca16bcb8736f","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To explore texture in music
  • To begin to develop creative thinking through composition
  • To perform a ‘spoken chorus’ or rap, in time as an ensemble
","title":"What’s achievable","image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"df137ab081ed3958","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Pencil and paper

","title":"What you need","image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"41b946b93958a1de","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Explore the lyrics ‘the buds are busy blossoming and blooming’, ‘it’s a bright and breezy, nice and easy feeling’, ‘daffodils-as-far-as-you-can-see thing’, ‘skip-along-the-road-and-hum-a-tune thing’, ‘feather-duster-whistle-while-you’re-cleaning’ and ‘creepy-caterpillar-buzzy-bee thing’.

Speak them rhythmically, as they are sung in the song, and at different dynamic levels e.g. loudly, moderately loudly, quietly. Split the class into small groups. To keep in time, have one group as a steady crotchet pulse repeating ‘buds are blooming’ over and over. Another group then repeats ‘the buds are busy blossoming and blooming’ rhythmically over the top. A third group can then add another phrase or ’layer’ to the texture, e.g. ‘it’s a bright and breezy, nice and easy feeling’.

Then ask each group to compose a ‘spoken chorus’ or rap, using some or all of these phrases, lasting between 30 seconds and a minute. They will need to think about how many times each phrase is repeated, varying the texture by using solos and/or duet sections, dynamics, the ensemble skills of coming in together (perhaps having a conductor) and staying in time. They may need to write down who does what and when! They could also include body percussion such as stamping, clapping or clicking fingers as a pulse to help them keep to the beat. Can they perform their compositions to the class?

","title":"","background_color":""}},{"key":"cf1a5d2a3d273472","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

For inspiration, listen to the beginning of The Geographical Fugue by Ernst Toch. Can they hear each of the four vocal parts or ‘layers’ come in? Listen out for the accented ‘Trinidad’ each time.

","title":"Listen","image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"4124ab4b8a94a813","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DcTEQi-4VAQ","title":"The Geographical Fugue","background_color":""}}]
resources.summary: Compose and perform a ‘spoken chorus’ or rap using lyrical phrases from It’s A Spring Thing!

resources.title: Playing Classical Music (Spring)
resources.content:
[{"key":"8de421d31e95fe11","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Make it a routine to play some classical music at the beginning of the day – perhaps when the children are taking off their coats, settling in the classroom or entering an assembly. Here are a few ideas: 

  • Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks (Mussorgsky)
  • The Lark Ascending (Vaughan-Williams)
  • On Hearing the First Cuckoo in Spring (Delius) 
  • Spring from The Four Seasons (Vivaldi) 
","title":"Music","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

resources.title: The Arrival Of Spring
resources.content:
[{"key":"e6936f3f06a10794","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

David Hockney (b. 1937) recently made a series of works responding to the changing colours of woodland (Wold Woods, Yorkshire) throughout the four seasons. He created oil paintings, charcoal drawings and iPad drawings, and recorded films as part of this series of work. 

How could the children use the influence of Hockney's work to respond to the colours and changing nature of spring? 

  • Take photos of the school grounds (field/flower beds/nature area) thoughout the seasons to see how things have grown and changed. (Record in a school/class calendar to carry on throughout the year.)
  • Record films of the school grounds. 
  • Incorporate technology to embrace Hockney's style: use iPads or tablets to create spring drawings and play back the creation of these to watch how they form the finished work. 
","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

Can the class identify when the key change occurs and stand up as they hear it? <\/p>\n","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":""}},{"key":"0c9521cba616a0f0","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https:\/\/music.youtube.com\/watch?v=vfxQ1oDiEJM&list=RDAMVMvfxQ1oDiEJM","title":"Penny Lane","noMargin":false}},{"key":"8ba68368c8021f6b","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https:\/\/music.youtube.com\/watch?v=K3BD6NQCGrA&list=RDAMVMK3BD6NQCGrA","title":"Livin' On A Prayer","noMargin":false}},{"key":"7051632c7e1a563b","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https:\/\/music.youtube.com\/watch?v=cQWY-bTSwtI&list=RDAMVMcQWY-bTSwtI","title":"Perfect Illusion ","noMargin":false}}]

resources.title: Planting Project
resources.content:
[{"key":"b1349c66455145d6","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Abraham Cruzvillegas (b. 1968) is a conceptual artist who creates sculptures and installations using found, recycled objects. 

In homage to Cruzvillegas' Empty Lot exhibition at Tate Modern, organize a planting project; ask the children to bring a small plant from their garden or a seed or a bulb from home. Find an area in the school garden, or use a colletion of indoor pot plants for the classroom. Plant the bulbs and seeds and study their growth throughout the season. Think about whether this could be photographed or recorded some way through drawing. How could you make it into a sculptural project? 

","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

resources.title: Longer Than The Line Before!
resources.content:
[{"key":"1043434ca7e1ce58","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Ideal for 2 sessions

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"af17acc9778b57da","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To describe the shape of a melody
  • To use graphic notation to represent pitch
  • To recognize the structure of a cumulative song
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"90889e93ce24821b","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

1p coins or buttons

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"20745f68279d6d9d","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Scale patterns; cumulative structure; direction; pitch; melody; melodic contour; rhythm; ascending; descending; tempo

","title":"Key vocabulary","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/icons-keyvocab-280x280-27-1620218359Ng3ET.png"}},{"key":"166044f59b07e54e","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

In The Jungle is a great song for exploring changes in pitch and getting the class to recognize scale patterns in music. The song also has a cumulative structure where an additional line is added to each verse, making every verse one line longer than the one before! Once the class knows the song well, focus on verse one and practise the last line (‘With a me, me, me...’). Listen to how the melody moves up and down the scale. It goes quite fast, so the class will have to listen carefully!

Can the children use their hands to follow the direction of the melody while they sing, showing you where the pitch gets higher or lower?

Next, show the class a set of coins or buttons. Sing the melody of the final line again, drawing its shape in the air. Now, try creating that melodic shape (contour) using the coins/buttons.

You might like to begin by clapping the rhythm of the words to work out how many coins/buttons are needed, and then arrange them to reflect the ascending and descending scale pattern.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"7675d1395b50629b","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/Year4/year4-musiccurr-longerthanthelinebefore-16394786345kFmO.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"442193f2e38dc2fe","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Sing the melody again, following the notation.

Can the children describe the shape of the melody? Can they identify the highest and lowest notes?

Next, listen to the second verse of the song. Notice how a line has been added. Sing the final two lines of the verse. Can the children follow the direction of the melody with their hands as they sing? They should notice how the melody moves up and down, forming a zigzag shape. What will the notation look like now? Work together to represent the melody using the coins/buttons.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"04cb51716b9a14a7","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/Year4/year4-musiccurr-longerthanthelinebefore2-1639478635tJN7N.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"1ab1eadaebb35a83","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Repeat the activity for the remaining verses. The children should start to spot the patterns and predict the overall shape (contour) of the melody. By the final verse, the coin/button notation should look like this:

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"555d1133511ab2ac","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/Year4/year4-musiccurr-longerthanthelinebefore3-1639478636msFCT.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"ba1817032a59fa2f","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Use tuned percussion instruments such as chime bars, boomwhackers or xylophones and select the notes B, C, D, E and F to form a five-note scale. Play up and down the scale a few times and hopefully, the class will recognize it as the ascending and descending melody from the song. Work together to identify the pitches of the first two notes (D and C) and then ask for volunteers to play the complete melody from the last line of the first verse. They will need to play the melody at a slower tempo.

","title":"Step It Up!","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1873-1614695091mFFrP.png"}},{"key":"c58e71df166ad72b","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/Year4/year4-musiccurr-longerthanthelinebefore4-163947863769wBk.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"43f12dbbaf24317c","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

There are many songs that use a cumulative structure. One of the most famous is the well-known Christmas song The Twelve Days Of Christmas.

","title":"Listen","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"c14aae1fecf03eb4","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2czHyicFqoY","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"46db1f4d9fec919a","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Explore songs with a cumulative structure. The Mad Moon Song, The Marching Band, In My Garden, It's A Spring Thing!, The Harvest List and I Got A Little Dog are all great songs to try.

","title":"Branch Out","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1874-1614695090s5QJx.png"}},{"key":"d5c7a07856800edc","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"ASSESSMENT SUGGESTIONS","background_color":"#009CCF"}},{"key":"c9d07658229516cd","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"
  • Can they identify and describe the direction of a melody (e.g. ascending, descending)?
  • Can they use graphic notation to represent ascending and descending melodies?
  • Can they recognize the structure of a cumulative song?
","title":"","noMargin":false}}]
